How to Hire a Google Trusted Photographer Today

Quick answer: To hire a Google Trusted photographer today, use the phrase as a legacy search term, not proof of a current Google credential. Find independent 360 photographers, send the same project brief to a short list, inspect recent work, compare written scopes and confirm who controls the files and published imagery before booking.[2][3][4]

Start with the 360 Photographer Directory search. If you are still deciding where to look, use our guide to finding a Google Trusted photographer. For the history behind the name, read what Google Street View Trusted Photographer means today.

Last reviewed: September 2026.

Write the project brief first

A useful quote starts with a useful brief. Send every candidate the same facts so you can compare like with like:

  • property address and type of business;
  • spaces that need to be photographed;
  • interior, exterior or both;
  • preferred date and any access restrictions;
  • intended publishing destination;
  • whether you need source files, a hosted tour or Street View publishing;
  • privacy, staging or safety requirements;
  • target delivery date.

You do not need to design the shoot yourself. The brief gives the photographer enough context to propose coverage and identify questions before pricing the work.

If you are unsure what a service package may contain, review what to expect from a Google Maps virtual tour service before requesting estimates.

Build a short list

Use the directory to identify several photographers who work in the project area. Directory profiles can help you compare location, specialties, portfolio information, equipment, hours, ratings and contact details.[1][2][5]

A short list is more useful than a long collection of names. Keep candidates whose work resembles the property type and scale you need. For a multi-location assignment, ask whether one photographer covers every site or whether the project will involve several local professionals.

Do not book from a title or badge alone. A person may accurately describe past participation in Google's former Trusted program, but Google no longer presents that program as an active certification or public hiring directory.[3]

Check recent, relevant work

Ask for two or three current examples that are close to your assignment. Open the tours rather than relying only on screenshots.

Look for:

  • sharp panoramas with level horizons;
  • consistent exposure and color;
  • sensible movement between viewpoints;
  • coverage that includes the spaces a visitor would expect;
  • careful handling of mirrors, windows and privacy-sensitive details;
  • a finished experience that works on both phone and desktop.

The date matters. Old work can show experience, but recent work is a better check on the photographer's current process and output.

Ask who captured and published each example. This avoids confusing a photographer's own project with work produced by another company or subcontractor.

Compare written scopes

A low quote may cover less work. A high quote may include services you do not need. Ask each candidate to itemize the same categories:

Scope item Decision to record
Capture plan Areas and approximate number of shooting positions
Editing Stitching, leveling, color work and privacy treatment
Publishing Whether Google Maps or Street View publishing is included
Hosted tour Whether a separate interactive tour is included
Source files Which original and edited files you receive
Account control Which account owns or controls the published contribution
Revisions Corrections and reshoots included in the price
Travel Mileage, transport, parking, permits or accommodation
Schedule Shoot date, delivery target and review window
Payment Deposit, milestone and final-payment terms

Google's current Street View contribution guidance describes ways to publish eligible 360 imagery, including Street View Studio and compatible software.[3] Publishing access is separate from the former Trusted badge, so ask about the actual workflow the photographer will use.

Confirm ownership and future access

Ownership questions are easy to postpone and difficult to fix later. Put the answers in writing before the shoot:

  1. Who receives the original panorama files?
  2. Who controls the account used for publishing?
  3. Can your organization retain copies of the edited assets?
  4. Who can correct, move or remove imagery later?
  5. Is a hosted tour tied to an ongoing hosting arrangement?
  6. What happens if the photographer becomes unavailable?

The correct arrangement depends on the project. The important part is that the client and photographer agree before publication.

Watch for claims Google warns about

Google's fraud-prevention guidance states that it does not employ photographers or agencies for these arrangements. It also warns against claims that imply Google endorsement or guarantee prominent placement in Search, Maps or Street View.[4]

Pause the conversation if a seller:

  • claims to be a Google employee while selling the service;
  • presents the old badge as a newly issued certification;
  • promises a guaranteed search or map ranking;
  • refuses to identify deliverables or account control;
  • cannot show recent work;
  • pressures you to buy before providing a written scope.

Historical experience can be relevant. It should be described with dates and supported by current work.

Make the booking decision

Compare the candidates against the same four questions:

  1. Does the portfolio match the assignment?
  2. Does the written scope cover the required work?
  3. Are control, revisions and future access clear?
  4. Can the photographer meet the location and schedule requirements?

Record the selected scope, location, access contact, price, payment schedule and delivery dates. If several sites are involved, add a site list and local contact for each one.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Google Trusted Photographer still a current certification?

No. Google's former program and hiring directory are no longer presented as active. Current publishing tools do not confer a new Google certification or endorsement.[3][4]

Does Google employ the photographer I hire?

No. Google says photographers and agencies are independent entities and that negotiations happen without Google's participation.[4]

How many photographers should I contact?

There is no required number. Contact enough suitable candidates to compare recent work, availability and a written scope. For a straightforward local job, a small short list is usually easier to evaluate than dozens of profiles.

Should I choose the lowest quote?

Compare included work before comparing totals. Capture, editing, publishing, source files, travel and revisions may differ between quotes.

Can a photographer guarantee better Google rankings?

No. Google warns against promises of prominent placement in Google Search, Maps or Street View.[4]

Where do I start?

Open the photographer search, choose your location and save the profiles that fit the project.[2]

Find candidates for your project

Search the 360 Photographer Directory, create a focused short list and send each photographer the same brief.[2]

The former badge may explain part of a photographer's history. The booking decision should rest on current work, a clear scope and an agreement you can refer to later.

Find a Google Trusted Photographer Near You

Quick answer: To find a Google Trusted photographer, search the independent 360 Photographer Directory by city, country or map area. Open several profiles, check the listed service area and portfolio, and save a short list of people who can handle the location and type of project you have.[1][2][5]

The word "Trusted" is a legacy search term. Google's current Street View contribution page no longer presents the former program as an active certification or official hiring list.[3] The directory gives you a current way to discover independent 360 photographers.

Search photographers by location.

Last reviewed: September 2026.

Start with the place, not the photographer's title

A photography project happens at a real address. Begin with the city or region where the camera work must take place.

Open the directory search and enter a location. You can use the list and map to see profiles associated with the area shown.[2] If your first search is too narrow, expand in this order:

  1. exact city;
  2. nearby cities or metropolitan area;
  3. state, province or region;
  4. country;
  5. a wider map area that a travelling photographer could cover.

This sequence keeps the first results practical while giving you room to find specialists outside the immediate city.

Use the map for geographic fit

The map is useful when the assignment sits between cities, covers a rural area or includes several nearby properties. Pan to the project area and review the photographers that appear in view.[2]

A marker or city label is a discovery signal, not a promise of availability. Confirm whether the photographer serves the exact address, whether travel is required and whether travel costs affect the quote.

For a multi-location project, make a simple location table before contacting anyone:

Location Preferred date Local access contact Candidate profiles
Site 1
Site 2
Site 3

The table shows where one photographer may cover several sites and where you may need local coverage.

Read directory profiles with a purpose

The directory is built to help clients compare individual 360 photographers. Its public description says profiles can include portfolios, specialties, hours, equipment, recent work, reviews, ratings and direct contact information.[5]

Use those fields to answer specific questions:

  • Check whether the listed location is close to the assignment or whether travel is likely.
  • Look for specialties that match the property or project type.
  • Open portfolio work that resembles your assignment.
  • Check whether the profile includes current work or recent updates.
  • Confirm that there is a direct route for discussing availability and scope.

Profile information helps you decide whom to contact. It does not replace a direct conversation about the assignment.

Search differently for one site and many sites

One local property

Prioritize geographic fit and recent examples from similar businesses. A local photographer may know the access, weather and travel conditions that affect the shoot.

Several properties in one region

Look for candidates who can cover the route efficiently. Share the full location list at the start so the photographer can assess travel and scheduling.

Properties in different countries

Use the directory separately for each market. Keep the project brief, shot expectations and file requirements consistent so work from different photographers can be compared and coordinated.

A specialist assignment

Start with the specialty, then confirm travel. A candidate outside the city may still be the better choice if the project requires unusual equipment, difficult lighting or experience with a specific property type.

Build a short list without over-researching

Save profiles that meet three basic conditions:

  1. plausible service coverage;
  2. relevant work you can inspect;
  3. a working contact route.

Remove profiles that clearly do not fit. There is little value in comparing dozens of candidates when only a few cover the place and project type.

Once you have a short list, move to the buyer process in How to Hire a Google Trusted Photographer Today. That guide covers the project brief, quote comparison, deliverables, account control and booking decision without repeating the directory search steps.

If your search shows few results

Broaden the map area or search a larger nearby city. A photographer may cover your location even if the profile is associated with another city.

You can also use the directory's contact page to ask for help finding a photographer in the project area.[6] Include the city or region, property type and preferred schedule so the request can be routed more efficiently.

Do not assume that no visible result means no photographer can take the job. It only means the current search did not surface a clear match.

What “Google Trusted” tells you and what it does not

Some photographers may have real history in Google's former Street View Trusted program. That history can be relevant, but the phrase no longer identifies a current Google certification or official directory.[3]

Google's fraud-prevention guidance also states that photographers and agencies are independent entities, not Google employees.[4] The 360 Photographer Directory is independent as well.[1][5]

For the complete explanation, read Google Street View Trusted Photographer: What It Means Today.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find a Google Trusted photographer near me?

Search the directory by city, region or country, then use the map to review nearby profiles. Confirm the exact service area directly with each photographer.[2]

Can I search outside my city?

Yes. Expand to nearby cities, a wider map area or the country level. Ask whether travel is available and how it affects the quote.

Does a directory profile mean Google recommends the photographer?

No. The directory is independent, and Google states that photographers and agencies are independent entities rather than Google employees.[4][5]

What should I compare first?

Start with location, relevant portfolio work and a direct contact route. Move to price and contract details after you have a realistic short list.

Where can I compare quotes and deliverables?

Use the separate hiring checklist after finding candidates. It covers scope, publishing, source files, revisions and account control.

What if I need a Google Maps virtual tour rather than general 360 photography?

Read what a Google Maps virtual tour service can include, then ask candidates whether they provide the required capture, editing and publishing work.

Search your project location

Open the 360 Photographer Directory, enter the location and build a short list from the profiles that fit.[2]

Search broadly enough to find the right skill, but keep the final list focused on people who can realistically serve the address.

Google Street View Trusted Photographer: What It Means Today

Definition: A Google Street View Trusted Photographer was a photographer recognized under Google's former Street View Trusted program. The designation and public for-hire list are no longer presented as active. Photographers can still create and publish eligible 360 imagery, but current publishing tools do not grant a new Trusted badge or Google endorsement.[3][4]

The phrase remains useful because clients still search for it. On this site, it points to experienced independent 360 photographers. It does not name a current Google certification.

Find 360 photographers by location.[2]

Last reviewed: September 2026.

The former program and the current situation

Google's former program recognized photographers who met its conditions. It also supported a public route for finding participating professionals. Some photographers earned the badge while the program was active and may accurately include that history in a profile.

Google now directs former Trusted program URLs to its general Street View contribution page. The current page explains cameras, capture and publishing options. It does not offer new Trusted Photographer enrollment or a current Google-operated hiring directory.[3]

The underlying service continues. Eligible imagery can still be contributed to Google Maps and Street View. The retired designation and the current contribution workflow are separate facts.

Legacy designation versus current evidence

Question Historical Trusted program Current hiring decision
What did it show? The photographer met the former program's conditions at that time The photographer's present work, process and fit
Can it be newly earned? Not through a current enrollment route No new badge is created by publishing imagery
Who employs the photographer? The photographer or agency operated independently Photographers and agencies remain independent entities
What should a client verify? Dates and accuracy of historical participation Portfolio, service area, deliverables, publishing experience and control
Where can clients search? The former Google for-hire route is no longer active Independent directories and direct referrals

A historical badge can be part of a professional record. It is not proof that every current project, service or claim has been reviewed by Google.

What a Street View photographer can still do

Google's current materials describe ways to capture and publish 360 imagery. Street View Studio supports eligible 360 video. Google Maps Help also explains how to publish and connect Photo Spheres through current Google and third-party workflows.[3][8]

Current services vary. They may include:

  • planning coverage for a business or location;
  • capturing 360 panoramas or video;
  • stitching and correcting images;
  • preparing imagery for publishing;
  • linking Photo Spheres through a supported third-party tool;
  • publishing or assisting with publication;
  • delivering original or edited files;
  • producing a separately hosted virtual tour.

These are service capabilities, not a new certification. Ask the photographer which parts are included rather than assuming the old title defines the package.

Photographers are independent from Google

Google's fraud-prevention guidance says it does not employ photographers or agencies. It also says these professionals are independent entities and warns against branding or claims that suggest Google endorsement.[4]

That means a photographer should not imply that Google:

  • employs them for your project;
  • participates in the contract or negotiation;
  • guarantees their service;
  • guarantees prominent placement in Search, Maps or Street View;
  • endorses their company because they can publish imagery.

A buyer should contract directly with the photographer or agency and record the scope, price and responsibilities independently.

How photographers should describe past participation

Clear wording protects both the photographer and the client. A historically accurate profile might say:

Previously recognized under Google's former Street View Trusted program.

It should not say:

Currently Google-certified or Google-endorsed.

Where possible, add the year or period of participation. Then support the historical note with recent work, current services, location coverage and a direct contact route.

Photographers should also avoid using Google brands in a way that suggests endorsement. Google's policy restricts the use of its trademarks, logos and Street View branding for that purpose.[4]

How clients should interpret the term

When a profile uses "Google Trusted Photographer," ask two separate questions:

  1. Is the historical statement accurate?
  2. Is this photographer right for the current assignment?

The second question deserves most of your attention. Review current examples, location coverage and the actual service package.

For local discovery, use Find a Google Trusted Photographer Near You. Once you have candidates, use How to Hire a Google Trusted Photographer Today for the brief, quote and account-control questions.

Better current terms

The right phrase depends on what you need:

  • 360 photographer for general immersive photography;
  • Street View contributor for someone who creates eligible imagery for Street View;
  • Google Maps virtual tour service provider for a business tour capture and publishing assignment;
  • virtual tour photographer when the project may include a separately hosted tour;
  • previously recognized under Google's former Street View Trusted program when historical participation is verified.

These terms describe the present service more accurately than treating the former badge as active.

Frequently asked questions

Is Google Street View Trusted Photographer still an active certification?

No. Google no longer presents an enrollment route, active badge program or official public hiring directory. Former program pages now lead to current contribution information.[3]

Did Google Street View stop accepting contributed imagery?

No. Google continues to describe ways to capture and publish eligible 360 imagery.[3][8]

Does publishing Street View imagery make someone Google-certified?

No. Publishing access is not a replacement certification program and does not create Google endorsement.[3][4]

Does Google employ independent Street View photographers?

No. Google's current guidance says photographers and agencies are independent entities, not Google employees.[4]

Can someone still mention the former badge?

Yes, when the claim is historically accurate and clearly dated. It should not be phrased as a current certification.

Where can I find a photographer now?

Use the independent 360 Photographer Directory to search by location and review profiles.[1][2]

What if I need a business virtual tour?

Read Google Maps Virtual Tour Service: What Businesses Should Expect to define the deliverables before contacting providers.

Find current 360 professionals

The old program name can still lead you to the right category of professional, but the decision should use current evidence.

Search the independent directory, review recent work and contact photographers who cover your project location.[2]

[2] https://360photographers.org/find-google-trusted-photographers — Find Photographers

[4] https://www.google.com/streetview/policy/fraud-prevention — Street View fraud prevention

Google Maps Virtual Tour Service: What Businesses Should Expect

Quick answer: A Google Maps virtual tour service usually combines professional 360 capture with image preparation and a plan for publishing eligible imagery to Google Maps or Street View. Some providers also deliver original files or build a separate hosted virtual tour. Confirm each deliverable in writing because capture, publishing and hosted-tour production are not automatically the same service.[3][7][8]

Google says on its current Street View business page that businesses can publish imagery themselves or work with a professional.[7] The 360 Photographer Directory helps you find independent professionals by location.[1][2]

Last reviewed: September 2026.

What the service can include

A provider may handle one part of the project or the full path from planning to delivery. A complete proposal can include:

  1. project planning and access coordination;
  2. 360 capture at the business location;
  3. stitching, leveling and image correction;
  4. privacy review and necessary blurring;
  5. preparation for Google Maps or Street View;
  6. publication or publishing assistance;
  7. original and edited file delivery;
  8. a separately hosted interactive tour;
  9. revisions, updates or a return visit.

Do not assume every proposal includes all nine. Ask the provider to mark each item as included, optional or excluded.

Google Maps imagery and a hosted virtual tour are different deliverables

The phrase "virtual tour" is used for more than one output. Decide which one the business needs.

Deliverable Where people view it Typical purpose Questions to ask
Google Maps or Street View imagery Within Google's Maps and Street View experiences Let people explore eligible published imagery associated with a place or route Who publishes it, which account controls it and how updates are handled?
Separately hosted virtual tour A provider or client-controlled web URL, often embedded on a website Provide a custom tour experience that may include branding, navigation or other presentation features Who hosts it, what features are included and what happens if hosting ends?
Delivered panorama files Client storage or another production workflow Preserve source material for reuse, archiving or future publishing Which originals and edited files are delivered, and under what usage rights?

Google explains that Photo Spheres can be published and connected through current Google and third-party workflows.[8] A hosted tour can be valuable too, but it should not be described as automatically published to Google Maps.

How a business virtual tour project works

1. Scope the location

The provider needs the address, type of business, spaces to include and any areas that must stay private. Larger or more complex locations may need a floor plan or a short planning call.

Discuss entrances, customer routes, floors, outdoor areas and accessibility points. Google's business guidance specifically describes using imagery to show a storefront, parking or an accessible entrance, as well as interior facilities before a visit.[7]

2. Prepare the space

Schedule the shoot when the location can be shown safely and without unnecessary interruption. Remove confidential material, confirm permission for restricted areas and decide how people will be kept out of the capture path where practical.

Ask who is responsible for final staging. A photographer can control the camera and production, but the business usually knows which displays, rooms or operational details should be visible.

3. Capture connected viewpoints

The photographer records a series of 360 viewpoints that represent the visitor path. The required number depends on the size and layout of the space.

For connected Photo Spheres, Google's guidance recommends clear lines of sight and spacing that supports movement between images.[8] The provider should explain the proposed coverage rather than selling an unexplained number of panoramas.

4. Prepare and review the imagery

Post-production may include stitching, leveling, exposure correction, color work and privacy treatment. Ask whether the business receives a review copy before publication and how corrections are requested.

A review stage is especially useful for mirrors, windows, people, license plates, screens and confidential information. Record who gives final approval.

Google's privacy guidance for contributed imagery distinguishes video from non-video submissions. Google applies automatic face and license-plate blurring to Street View made from user-submitted 360 video, but not to non-video imagery such as Photo Spheres. For still panoramas, confirm who will inspect and blur sensitive details before publication.[9]

5. Publish and hand off

Google's Street View contribution materials describe Street View Studio and compatible third-party tools for current publishing workflows.[3][8] The provider should identify the method that fits the imagery and project.

The handoff should state:

  • what was published;
  • which account controls the contribution;
  • which files the client receives;
  • whether a hosted tour has a separate URL or subscription;
  • who handles corrections and future updates;
  • how long review copies and source files are retained.

What the service should not promise

Google's fraud-prevention guidance states that photographers and agencies are independent entities. It warns against claims of Google employment, endorsement or guaranteed prominent placement in Search, Maps or Street View.[4]

A responsible proposal should not promise:

  • a promised position in Google Search;
  • a guaranteed number of views or leads;
  • Google employment or participation in the contract;
  • a newly issued Trusted Photographer certification;
  • permanent hosting or publication without defining the responsible platform and terms.

The service can produce and publish useful imagery. Business outcomes still depend on the location, audience, wider marketing and Google's own systems.

Information to prepare before requesting a quote

Send providers a short service brief:

  • business name and address;
  • property type and approximate size;
  • rooms, floors and outdoor areas to include;
  • dates and access windows;
  • current imagery that needs replacement or updating;
  • Google Maps or Street View publishing needs;
  • hosted-tour requirements, if any;
  • original-file and usage-right requirements;
  • privacy or security restrictions;
  • target date and approval contact.

This information helps the provider estimate the capture plan, travel, editing and delivery work.

For the full candidate and quote process, use How to Hire a Google Trusted Photographer Today.

Cost factors

There is no single standard price for a Google Maps virtual tour service. Quotes can vary with:

  • location size and layout;
  • number of viewpoints;
  • travel and access;
  • lighting or staging complexity;
  • editing and privacy work;
  • publishing support;
  • hosted-tour production;
  • file delivery and usage terms;
  • revisions, reshoots and future updates.

Ask for an itemized proposal. It is easier to compare providers when capture, editing, publishing, hosting and travel are listed separately.

Keeping imagery current

A remodel, new entrance, changed floor plan or updated customer area can make older imagery less useful. Google's business guidance encourages organizations to keep imagery current when the location changes.[7]

Before the first project ends, ask how updates are priced and who can manage the existing imagery. Keep the source files, account details and written scope where future staff can find them.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Google Maps virtual tour service?

It is a professional service for planning, capturing and preparing 360 imagery, often with publication to Google Maps or Street View. The exact package may also include source files or a separately hosted tour.

Is a hosted virtual tour automatically added to Google Maps?

No. A hosted tour and Google-published imagery are separate outputs. A provider may offer both, but the proposal should name each deliverable.

Can a business publish imagery without hiring a professional?

Yes. Google provides current contribution paths for eligible imagery.[3][7] A professional may be useful when the location, quality requirements or production workload exceed the team's available equipment and time.

Is the provider employed or endorsed by Google?

No. Google says photographers and agencies are independent entities and restricts claims that imply endorsement.[4]

Will a virtual tour guarantee better search rankings?

No. Google warns against promises of prominent placement in Search, Maps or Street View.[4]

Who should control the published imagery?

The business and provider should agree on account control before publication. The proposal should also explain who handles later corrections or updates.

Where can I find a service provider?

Use the 360 Photographer Directory to search by location and review independent photographer profiles.[1][2]

Find a professional for the project

Define whether you need Google-published imagery, a hosted tour, delivered files or a combination. Then search the directory for professionals who cover the location.[2]

If a profile uses the former Google Trusted title, read what that designation means today before treating it as part of the decision.
